extracted.intended_audience: Fortune readers; general business/fashion audience; corporate PR and communications professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating or drafting a corporate public apology/press statement and corrective actions after an offensive product or PR misstep (fashion industry example). Focuses on content, timing, tone, and remedial measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express a clear, direct apology
rubrics_metrics.description: “We are deeply sorry for the distress caused by one of the products that featured in our A/W 2019 runway collection Tempest,” said Burberrry CEO Marco Gobbetti.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include an unambiguous statement of regret that acknowledges harm. Avoid vague or euphemistic language; state sorrow or apology explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate corrective action (remove product and images)
rubrics_metrics.description: “We immediately removed the product and all images that featured it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State concrete steps already taken (product removal, image takedown, recall) to show action, not just words. Be specific about what was removed and when.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct outreach to affected individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: “I called Ms. Kennedy to apologize as soon as I became aware of this on Monday…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contact directly anyone obviously harmed or who raised the concern; mention that outreach publicly if appropriate to show accountability and empathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge insensitivity and accept responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: “Though the design was inspired by the marine theme… it was insensitive and we made a mistake.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admit the error plainly instead of deflecting. Saying inspiration/context is acceptable only alongside explicit acceptance that the result was hurtful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide context/explanation without excusing the harm
rubrics_metrics.description: “While the design was inspired by a nautical theme, I realize that it was insensitive.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give brief context (design inspiration) to inform the public, but do not use it to excuse or minimize the impact; pair context with acknowledgement of fault.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commit to reflection and preventive measures
rubrics_metrics.description: “We will reflect on this, learn from it and put in place all necessary actions to ensure it does not happen again.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outline a promise to review policies/practices and implement changes; ideally follow up later with specifics on what was changed (process, approvals, training).

rubrics_metrics.name: Leadership accountability and personal responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Riccardo Tisci: “I am so deeply sorry for the distress… I will make sure that this does not happen again.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Senior leaders (CEO/creative director) should take visible responsibility rather than delegating blame; statements from leadership carry weight and should commit to concrete follow-through.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listen to and act on internal concerns (avoid dismissing staff/models)
rubrics_metrics.description: Model Liz Kennedy said her backstage objections were ignored and she was told to “write a letter” and “it’s fashion. Nobody cares…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dismiss internal complaints; establish channels for staff/models to raise and escalate concerns and show that internal warnings are heeded in decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be sensitive to subjects affecting vulnerable people or groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Kennedy: “Suicide is not fashion… It is not glamorous nor edgy… especially in a line dedicated to young girls and youth.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid imagery, words, or motifs that reference suicide, racial stereotypes, or other traumatic subjects—especially when marketing to youth or vulnerable audiences. Consider psychological and cultural impacts during design and review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of response
rubrics_metrics.description: CEO said he called and the product was removed as soon as he became aware.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond quickly once the issue is identified—delayed responses can amplify backlash. Timely apology plus action reduces harms and shows seriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about what happened and what was done
rubrics_metrics.description: Article notes apology, removal of item and images, and direct calls to the affected model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about the facts of the incident and the remedial steps taken; transparency builds trust. If ongoing investigation or policy changes are planned, say so and provide timelines where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate empathetic tone (avoid defensive framing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tisci: “It was never my intention to upset anyone. It does not reflect my values nor Burberry’s…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an empathetic tone that centers injured parties’ experiences rather than defending intent; acknowledging unintentional harm is fine but should not substitute for responsibility and remedial commitments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn from industry precedents and avoid repeat mistakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Article cites similar recent incidents at H&M, Groupon and Gap as comparable corporate missteps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of comparable public controversies and the lessons they offer; proactively audit product/content for foreseeable sensitivities to avoid repeating common pitfalls.
